idiom_name: module-level binding under the import lock (or a threading.Lock plus cached_property)
implementation_notes: Python has no once primitive, but it rarely needs one: a module body executes exactly once under the import machinery's per-module lock, so a module-level constant is the natural once-cell and `import` is the (implicit) synchronisation - which is why the idiomatic answer is to move the build to import time or into an lru_cache/cached_property memoizer rather than to sleep on a flag. Where laziness is genuinely required on shared state, write the lock explicitly: a module-level threading.Lock with the check repeated inside it (the second check is what makes the lock conditional, exactly as in the classic pattern). Note that under the GIL an unsynchronised `if _cfg is None: _cfg = build()` can still run the builder twice because the thread may switch between the test and the store - the reference store itself is atomic - and PEP 703 free-threaded builds remove even that comfort, so explicit locking becomes mandatory there.
code_sketch:
import threading

_config = None
_lock = threading.Lock()

def config() -> Config:
    global _config
    if _config is None:                 # fast path: one attribute read
        with _lock:
            if _config is None:         # only one thread builds
                _config = Config.load()
    return _config
pitfalls: Class-body and __init__ initialisation is eager and process-global: it runs at import time (so failures surface as a half-imported module) and tests cannot reset it without reloading the module.

functools.cached_property had an undocumented per-property lock to guarantee one run per instance and that locking was removed in Python 3.12, so concurrent first accesses may run the getter more than once; make the builder idempotent or guard it.
Assigning to an attribute backed by cached_property shadows the descriptor permanently, which silently disables it instead of invalidating it.
Under free-threaded CPython (PEP 703) the check-then-act idiom races for real: two threads can build two objects and discard one, so the explicit lock is not optional on those builds.
